
Spatial count data often have more zeros than a count distribution allows,
more variance than the mean, and dependence between neighbouring units: the
number of solar panels installed in a neighbourhood, of emergency visits from
a municipality, of firms of a sector in a district. The ZISAR model handles
the three at once, and **zisar** estimates it by maximum likelihood.

```{r setup}
library(zisar)
```

## The model

For \(n\) spatial units linked by a weights matrix \(W\) (row-standardised,
with zero diagonal), the log-mean of the counts follows a simultaneous
autoregressive (SAR) process with unit-level random effects,

\[
\eta = \rho W \eta + X\beta + u, \qquad u \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I),
\qquad\text{so}\qquad \eta = (I - \rho W)^{-1}(X\beta + u).
\]

Each count is a *structural zero* with probability \(\pi_i\), and otherwise
negative binomial with mean \(\mu_i = \exp(\eta_i)\) and shape \(\kappa\):

\[
y_i \sim \pi_i \, 1\{y_i = 0\} + (1 - \pi_i)\,\mathrm{NB}(\mu_i, \kappa),
\qquad \mathrm{logit}(\pi_i) = z_i'\gamma.
\]

The spatial multiplier \((I - \rho W)^{-1}\) acts on the *latent* predictor,
not on the observed counts, so the model has no endogenous regressor and is
estimated by maximum likelihood. Overdispersion has three sources: the
negative binomial shape \(\kappa\), the structural zeros \(\pi_i\) and the
random effects \(\sigma\). The latent field is integrated out with the
Laplace approximation in [TMB](https://cran.r-project.org/package=TMB).

This is the *restricted* model: the structural zeros depend on covariates
only. The *general* model adds a spatial field to the inflation predictor,
for zeros that cluster in space; see [below](#clustered-structural-zeros).

## Fitting a model

`rzisar()` simulates data on a regular lattice with queen contiguity. Here
400 units, a spatial parameter of 0.5, two covariates in the count process
and one in the zero-inflation process:

```{r simulate}
set.seed(2026)
sim <- rzisar(20, beta = c(0.5, 0.6, -0.4), rho = 0.5, gamma = c(-1, 0.9),
              kappa = 2, sigma = 0.4)
head(sim$data)
mean(sim$data$y == 0)
```

`zisar()` takes a two-part formula: the terms before `|` enter the count
process, those after it the zero-inflation process. `W` can be a base
matrix, a sparse `Matrix`, or an `spdep` `listw` object, with rows in the
order of the data.

```{r fit}
fit <- zisar(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = sim$data, W = sim$W)
summary(fit)
```

The estimates are close to the values used in the simulation
(\(\beta = (0.5, 0.6, -0.4)\), \(\gamma = (-1, 0.9)\), \(\rho = 0.5\),
\(\kappa = 2\), \(\sigma = 0.4\)). The usual accessors work:

```{r accessors}
coef(fit)
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))
logLik(fit)
AIC(fit)
```

A formula without `|` uses the same terms in both processes, `y ~ x | 1`
gives a constant inflation probability, and an `offset()` term in the count
part enters the log-mean with coefficient one, for exposures:
`y ~ x1 + offset(log(households)) | z1`.

## Spatial weights from real geography

With polygons, `spdep` builds the weights; pass the `listw` object (or the
matrix) to `zisar()`. Every unit must have a row in the data: units cannot
be dropped, because they all enter the spatial multiplier.

```{r spdep, eval = FALSE}
library(sf)
library(spdep)
areas <- st_read("areas.gpkg")
nb <- poly2nb(areas, queen = TRUE)
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
fit <- zisar(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = areas, W = lw)
```

## Direct, indirect and total effects

In a spatial model a coefficient is not the effect of its covariate: a
change in one unit moves the expected count there (direct effect) and, through
the spatial multiplier, in the other units (indirect effect, or spillover).
`zisar_effects()` averages them over units, with simulation standard errors:

```{r effects}
zisar_effects(fit, B = 100)
```

`z1` acts only through the probability of a structural zero, which concerns
the unit itself: its indirect effect is zero. A covariate entering both
processes (the same name in both parts of the formula) combines the two
channels.

## Counterfactual scenarios

`predict()` gives the fitted means (`type = "response"`), the means of the
count component (`"count"`), the inflation probabilities (`"zero"`) or the
latent field (`"eta"`). With `newdata` for the same units it computes a
scenario: here `x1` rises by one in a single unit, and the expected counts
of its neighbours rise as well.

```{r predict}
nd <- sim$data
nd$x1[190] <- nd$x1[190] + 1
change <- predict(fit, newdata = nd) - predict(fit)
round(change[c(190, which(sim$W[190, ] > 0))], 3)
sum(change)
```

## Comparing models

`fixed` holds parameters at given values. With \(\rho = 0\) and
\(\sigma\) close to zero the model reduces to the aspatial zero-inflated
negative binomial, the same model as `pscl::zeroinfl(dist = "negbin")`:

```{r nested}
fit_zinb <- zisar(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = sim$data, W = sim$W,
                  fixed = list(rho = 0, sigma = 0.001))
AIC(fit_zinb, fit)
```

The test of \(\rho = 0\) is in the summary (Wald). The aspatial model with
random effects (`fixed = list(rho = 0)`) is nested in ZISAR, but on
spatially dependent data it is often not estimable: the random effects have
to absorb the spatial structure, \(\sigma\) grows, and the Laplace
approximation breaks down (see below).

## Clustered structural zeros

In the restricted model, structural zeros depend on \(z_i\) only. When
whole areas are out of the market (a planning restriction, no supplier
nearby), the zeros cluster beyond what the covariates explain. The general
model gives the inflation predictor a SAR field of its own,

\[
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_i) = z_i'\gamma + g_i, \qquad
g = (I - \rho_0 W)^{-1} e_0, \qquad e_0 \sim N(0, \sigma_0^2 I),
\]

independent of \(u\). `rzisar()` draws it when `sigma0 > 0`, and
`zero_spatial = TRUE` fits it:

```{r general}
set.seed(2)
sim0 <- rzisar(15, beta = c(1, 0.5), rho = 0.4, gamma = c(-1, 0.8),
               rho0 = 0.6, sigma0 = 1)
fit_r <- zisar(y ~ x1 | z1, data = sim0$data, W = sim0$W)
fit_g <- zisar(y ~ x1 | z1, data = sim0$data, W = sim0$W,
               zero_spatial = TRUE)
summary(fit_g)$spatial
```

The restricted model is the general one with \(\sigma_0 = 0\), on the
boundary of the parameter space, so the likelihood-ratio statistic has a
mixture distribution and the \(\chi^2_2\) p-value is conservative:

```{r general-lr}
lr <- 2 * (logLik(fit_g) - logLik(fit_r))
pchisq(as.numeric(lr), df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

The two latent fields compete for the same zeros (a zero is either a
structural zero, with a large \(g_i\), or a negative binomial zero, with a
small \(\eta_i\)), so the general model is harder to estimate and more
exposed to the breakdown described next. Fit the restricted model first,
and read \(\rho_0\) and \(\sigma_0\) only from a general fit with
`laplace_ok = TRUE`.

## When the Laplace approximation breaks down

For a zero count, the conditional distribution of \(\eta_i\) can be bimodal:
the zero is either structural (and \(\mu_i\) can be large) or negative
binomial (and \(\mu_i\) is small). When \(\sigma\) is large this produces
spurious optima, with a huge gradient and sometimes a positive
log-likelihood. It happens mostly in small samples and with misspecified
models, for example with an omitted covariate. `zisar()` checks every fit,
restarts from other values when a check fails, and warns if no usable
optimum is found; `fit$laplace_ok` records the outcome and `summary()`
reports it.

```{r check}
fit$laplace_ok
fit$max_grad
```

## Large data sets

The log-determinant \(\log|I - \rho W|\) is computed from the eigenvalues of
\(W\) for up to 5000 units, and from a sparse Cholesky factorisation beyond
(`logdet = "sparse"`), which keeps memory and time manageable for tens of
thousands of units. `zisar_effects()` never forms the dense
\(n \times n\) multiplier either.

```{r large, eval = FALSE}
fit <- zisar(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = big, W = W_big, logdet = "sparse")
```

## Reference

Salvini, N., Arbia, G. and Nardelli, V. (2026). ZISAR: A zero-inflated
spatial autoregressive model for count data with random effects. Working
paper, Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore.
